summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but a visitor to Tacna faces a legal regime with no gender-identity-recognition law and no hate-crime statute. Anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label applied by investigators carries no separate legal consequence. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Access to public facilities is restricted by statute. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents mandates that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. A congressional committee approved unanimously in February 2025, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia. Activists in Tacna cite a legislative proposal by congressman Alejandro Muñante restricting access to public bathrooms as part of the environment they describe.

The restriction reaches private life as well as state facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed in Peru, trans women most affected. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The Public Prosecutor's Office identified 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021, of which 55.8% of victims were gay men and 36.4% trans women.

In Tacna, Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a hostel room on 19 April 2025. The autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways. She had entered the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone about two hours later; she was initially processed as NN and identified through the hostel's cameras, and police analysed surveillance footage inside and outside the building to trace his escape route. As of 21 May 2025 no suspect had been identified, and the Public Prosecutor's Office was investigating the killing as a possible hate crime, meaning an offence motivated by prejudice and discrimination on grounds of the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity.

Her family and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil in Tacna on 23 May 2025 demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. Relatives had earlier denounced the crime and demanded police action.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Peru stands out within its subregion on hate-crime coverage: with Paraguay and Guyana it is one of only three South American countries whose hate-crime law carries no LGBT anti-discrimination provision. The gap runs against the direction of the regional human-rights framework set by Advisory Opinion OC-24/17.

Recorded figures understate the harm. Gianna Camacho's caution that the 2024 report's figures are a sub-registry, combined with the initial NN classification of the Tacna victim and the absence of an identified suspect three days after the body was found, indicates that both the incidence and the clearance rate of anti-trans killings are uncertain.

The 'hate crime' designation applied by prosecutors in the Tacna case is investigative framing rather than a distinct offence, so a conviction would rest on ordinary homicide or asphyxia-related charges. The Azul Rojas Marín judgment shows how long redress has taken in practice: roughly two decades from attack to a 17-year sentence, obtained only after the case travelled through the Inter-American Commission to the regional Court.

Facility restrictions have already been applied beyond state buildings, as the dismissed gym complaint shows, and public figures have invoked the men's-room rule as a rhetorical device against LGBT legislators. The legislative package also reaches signage and media content, so visible markers of inclusion carry legal exposure.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tacna live under the national framework without a local ordinance of their own: the bathroom rule, the signage ban and the raised obscenity minimum derive from the April 2025 national law, and the 2017 repeal of LGBT hate-crime coverage applies in the department as elsewhere in Peru.

Local LGTBIQ+ collectives organised the 23 May 2025 vigil for Marcia Paucara Cora and have pressed the Public Prosecutor's Office on the case, framing the killing within a structural pattern rather than as an isolated act. Relatives reported the crime to police and asked for action while the victim was still unidentified.

Health practice changed for residents in June 2024, when national health authorities dropped pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance, improving how trans patients are treated in clinical settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree after an activist challenge, a precedent available to litigants nationwide.

Congressman Alejandro Muñante's bathroom-access proposal and the Montoya bills show that further restrictive measures remain in the legislative pipeline, so the current statutory position may tighten rather than loosen.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Tacna investigation produced a named suspect, an arrest or charges after 21 May 2025 is unresolved in the available sources; the latest account records only that no suspect had been identified and that footage was still being analysed.

Wayka describes the Muñante bathroom proposal as a 'recently promulgated legislative proposal', wording that does not establish whether it was enacted as law or merely reported to plenary. Its current legal status is unresolved here.

Whether the consumer-protection body's dismissal of the gym complaint was final or subject to appeal is not sourced. Nor is it sourced whether the Tacna case has since been reclassified, or what charge would ultimately be brought given the absence of a hate-crime statute.

The 84 complaints recorded by the Public Prosecutor's Office cover January 2012 to May 2021 and predate the 2024 and 2025 reporting; the sources do not reconcile them with the 54 killings counted for 2020 to 2023, and no Tacna-specific breakdown of those complaints is available.

Local Tacna enforcement practice under the April 2025 facility rules, including how hostels, gyms and municipal buildings apply the biological-sex criterion, is not documented in the inventory.
